{{China divisions by}}

The article is about [[China]]'s [[Province-level divisions of China|first-level]] [[Administrative divisions of China|administrative divisions]] by their [[gross domestic product]] per capita for selected years. All figures are given in the national currency, [[renminbi]] (CNY) and in [[United States dollar|USD]], at nominal values. [[Purchasing power parity]] (PPP) indicators, which are measured in [[international dollar]]s and fluctuate frequently, and PPP data is not included in the main table, only included at the end of the entry. Purchasing power parity reference comes from the [[World Economic Outlook]] published by the [[International Monetary Fund]] (IMF). The [[list of renminbi exchange rates|average CNY exchange rate]] used here is from [[National Bureau of Statistics of China|China NBS]], and [[List of renminbi exchange rates#List of purchasing power parity exchange rates|CNY PPP exchange rates]] are estimated according to the IMF.

Unless otherwise specified, GDP per capita is based on the annual average population. The annual average population, also referred to as the mid-year population, is calculated as the average of the resident populations at the end of two consecutive years.

Since the implementation of reform and opening-up in mainland China in 1978, its economy has developed rapidly. In 1995, the GDP per capita of Beijing, Tianjin, and Shanghai exceeded US$1,000; by 2000, 10 provinces had GDP per capita above US$1,000, of which Beijing, Tianjin, and Shanghai exceeded US$2,000. Per capita GDP surpassed US$10,000 for the first time in Beijing (US$10,402) and Shanghai (US$10,593) in 2009. Mainland China's per capita GDP (US$10,083) exceeded US$10,000 for the first time in 2018, and 11 provinces—including Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, Tianjin, Fujian, Zhejiang, Guangdong, Hubei, Chongqing,  Shandong and Inner Mongolia—had per capita GDP above US$10,000, with Beijing and Shanghai exceeding US$20,000 per capita in the same year. As of 2025, 22 provincial-level divisions in mainland China have a nominal GDP per capita above US$10,000, while 9 — including Yunnan, Qinghai, and Gansu — remain below this threshold. Beijing and Shanghai exceed US$30,000, and Jiangsu and Fujian have surpassed US$20,000.

Apart from the national capital, Beijing, and the financial capital, Shanghai, coastal provinces lead China's per capita GDP rankings, as they are most heavily exposed to [[export-oriented industrialization]]. The [[Port|seaports]] in these provinces provide greater exposure to [[international trade]] and allow both local and foreign companies, which receive [[Foreign direct investment in China|foreign direct investment]] (FDI) in China, to [[export|export goods]] and access [[global market|global markets]] more efficiently.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Felice |first1=Emanuele |last2=Odoardi |first2=Iacopo |last3=D’Ingiullo |first3=Dario |date=2021-09-18 |title=The Chinese Inland-Coastal Inequality: The Role of Human Capital and the 2007–2008 Crisis Watershed |journal=Italian Economic Journal |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=761–788 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s40797-021-00169-w |s2cid=240506688 |issn=2199-3238|doi-access=free }}</ref>

For comparison purposes, this article also presents the GDP of the [[Hong Kong]] and [[Macau]] [[Special administrative regions of China|Special Administrative Regions]] (SARs), which maintain [[Customs territory|separate economic systems]] and currencies. Likewise, GDP indicators for the two SARs are presented in local currency, U.S. dollars, and at [[purchasing power parity]], with PPP data sourced from the IMF.{{ref|A}}

* {{note|A}}All the comparative data for Chinese Yuan Renminbi is based on World Economic Outlook Database of the [[International Monetary Fund]].
* [[Mainland China]] figures were calculated by dividing figures in the [[list of Chinese provincial-level divisions by GDP]] by figures in the [[list of Chinese administrative divisions by population]].

{{Reflist|refs=
<ref name="China NBS GDP data">最新年份人均GDP基于各省统计公报公布的当年末人口与上年末人口平均数计算。其他历史年份各省人均GDP参考China NBS数据库。The latest GDP per capita figures are calculated based on the average of the year-end population published in the provincial statistical communiqué for that year and the year-end population for the previous year. For other historical years, GDP per capita for each province is referenced from the China NBS database. refer to China NBS National data {{cite press release | url=https://data.stats.gov.cn/english| title=regional - Annual by province - national accounts - gross regional product| publisher=China NBS|access-date=May 5, 2026}}</ref>

<ref name="IMFPPP">Purchasing power parity index reference to the {{cite press release | url=https://data.imf.org/en/datasets/IMF.RES:WEO | title=April 2026 World Economic Outlook | publisher=IMF |access-date= May 5, 2026}}</ref>

<ref name="population">China uses the calendar year as its fiscal year, its official GDP per capita is based on mid-year population. The mid-year population is the average at the end of the previous year and the end of the current year. Population of each province at the end of each year {{cite press release | url= https://data.stats.gov.cn/english/easyquery.htm?cn=E0102| title=Home - Regional - annual - population | publisher=China NBS}}</ref>

<ref name="EXrate">For the exchange rate of the latest year, refer to the Statistical Communiqué of that year {{cite press release | url=https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202602/t20260228_1962661.html| title=Statistical communiqué of the People's Republic of China on the national economic and social development| publisher=China NBS |date=February 28, 2026 |access-date=April 19, 2026}};  Refer to the national statistical database for the historical exchange rates {{cite press release | url=https://data.stats.gov.cn/english| title=national data - annual - foreign tarde and economic cooperation - reference exchange rate of renminbi (period average)| publisher=China NBS|access-date=April 19, 2026}}, and for the historical exchange rates also published on the statistical yearbooks {{cite press release | url=http://www.stats.gov.cn/sj/ndsj| title=statistical yearbooks (Chinese / English)| publisher=China NBS|access-date=April 19, 2026}}</ref>

<ref name="5th-economic-census">The economic data for 2023 and previous years were revised based on the 5th National Economic Census in 2023 and released by the National Bureau of Statistics of China {{cite press release | url=https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202501/t20250117_1958330.html| title=National Economy Witnessed Steady Progress amidst Stability with Major Development Targets Achieved Successfully in 2024| publisher=China NBS| date=January 17, 2025| access-date=November 11, 2025}}.</ref>

<ref name="HMT">Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan exist as separate customs territories, and their social and economic development indicators are not included in China's data. All data concerning these regions here references to the {{cite press release | url=https://data.imf.org/en/datasets/IMF.RES:WEO | title=April 2026 World Economic Outlook | publisher=IMF |access-date= May 5, 2026}} Their GDP data for Hong Kong and Macau are based on data released by the IMF; actual GDP per capita is calculated at year-end population. For the annual average exchange rate of local currency to Chinese yuan (CN¥‌), refer to chl.cn {{cite press release | url=https://chl.cn/huilv/ | title=zh: 汇率 | publisher=chl.cn|access-date= May 5, 2026}}; GDP figures based on local currency, US dollar, and purchasing power parity over the years, referenced from the IMF April 2026 World Economic Outlook<br>
